claims.text: The target material is a single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy at ambient conditions.
Adding DFT-calculated lattice-distortion and local-bonding descriptors to an ML model will reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to empirical or CALPHAD-based methods.
DFT can provide detailed phonon-dispersion information for use in a learned interatomic or predictive model.
DFT can provide reliable temperature-dependent lattice-distortion metrics for disordered CoCrFeMnNi alloys from ambient temperature to about 600 K.
DFT-derived data or descriptors can be incorporated into machine-learning property models.
Atomic-level lattice distortions and local bonding heterogeneity are relevant structural mediators in CoCrFeMnNi.
Severe lattice distortion in high-entropy materials reduces phonon group velocity.
Severe lattice distortion enhances phonon scattering and reduces phonon mean free path.
Increased phonon scattering caused by lattice distortion results in low intrinsic or lattice thermal conductivity.
Representing lattice-distortion and bonding effects with DFT descriptors and correlating them using ML will yield more precise quantitative thermal-conductivity predictions.
The model will identify a CoCrFeMnNi-based variant with thermal conductivity below 5 W/(m·K).
Conventional empirical and CALPHAD-based methods have higher prediction errors for CoCrFeMnNi because they inadequately represent complex lattice-distortion effects.
The proposed approach is applicable only to single-phase, near-equimolar CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys at temperatures no higher than about 600 K.
The approach may not transfer to multiphase alloys or compositions substantially different from equimolar CoCrFeMnNi.
DFT may not fully capture local chemical disorder and anharmonic phonon interactions in CoCrFeMnNi.
Laser flash analysis can directly provide phonon thermal conductivity for the synthesized alloy over the ambient-to-600 K range.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional predictions would falsify the hypothesis.
A measured thermal conductivity significantly above 5 W/(m·K) for the model-selected alloy would falsify the predicted low-conductivity outcome.
